A close reading for the week

“Morphine or cocaine?”

The Sign of Four · Chapter 1

The second Holmes novel opens with a syringe. Watson, a doctor, finally protests; Holmes, a mind with nothing to do, explains. The exchange fixed the character for a century, and it is Watson’s voice that carries the scene.

Again and again I had registered a vow that I should deliver my soul upon the subject, but there was that in the cool, nonchalant air of my companion which made him the last man with whom one would care to take anything approaching to a liberty.1 … Yet upon that afternoon, whether it was the Beaune which I had taken with my lunch, or the additional exasperation produced by the extreme deliberation of his manner, I suddenly felt that I could hold out no longer.

“Which is it to-day?” I asked,—“morphine or cocaine?”2

  1. 1

    The last man to take a liberty with

    Watson has watched the syringe three times a day “for many months” and said nothing. The reason is Holmes’s manner, “cool, nonchalant”, which forbids intimacy. The novel opens by establishing the distance between the two men, and the friendship as something Watson must find the courage to act on. The Beaune at lunch helps. It is a very human beginning for a book about a reasoning machine.

  2. 2

    Morphine or cocaine?

    The question is blunt and clinical, a doctor’s question, and the “to-day” tells us it is habitual. Both drugs were legal and available from chemists in 1890; cocaine had been isolated in the 1850s and was being promoted as a tonic. Doyle, a doctor himself, knew the pharmacology, and the famous opening is medically exact. Whatever shock it gave the first readers was moral; nothing here was against the law.
